body_markdown:
Pull your helmet off after a long ride and your ears are ringing, or the world sounds muffled for an hour before your ears go back to normal.


Wind roar under a full-face helmet hits roughly 90 dB(A) at 40 mph and climbs to about 112 dB(A) by 100 mph. At 112 dB(A), NIOSH's own exposure math gives you[under a minute before you've hit your safe daily limit](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/noise/about/noise.html) . Most riders blame their pipes, but wind is the real damage. Your helmet was built to survive a crash, not seal out sound. And overtime, that wind noise exposure could damage your ears for good,, whether you notice it or not.


## Wind Noise Hits 90 dB at 40 MPH: Your Helmet Won't Stop It


Past 40 mph, wind noise around your helmet outruns your engine, and keeps climbing from there. Acoustic testing from the[University of Southampton's Institute of Sound and Vibration Research (ISVR)](https://isvr.co.uk/projects/motorcycle-noise/) backs this up. Once you clear 40 mph, wind is the loudest thing on your ride, not your motor.


A[controlled study of the motorcyclist's riding environment](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8054899/) breaks it down by speed:


Riding Speed Wind Noise Under a Full-Face Helmet


40 mph ~90 dB(A)


Highway cruising (65–80 mph) Climbing past 100 dB(A)


100 mph ~112 dB(A)


### Your Helmet Doesn't Block Wind Noise


A full-face lid is built to survive an impact, not protect you from sound. Wearing a helmet with no hearing protection and you can still be sitting in 90+ dB(A) of wind roar on an ordinary highway stretch.


### The NIOSH Countdown


NIOSH sets 85 dB(A) as the safe limit over an 8-hour day, and every 3 dB above that cuts your safe exposure time in half. At 94 dB(A), that's down to one hour. Highway cruising speeds blow past that fast.


At highway speed, wind noise runs about 90 dB(A) at 40 mph and rises to roughly 112 dB(A) by 100 mph, past the exposure limits that cause permanent hearing damage.


Numbers like that should make riders think twice about using earplugs, but most skip them anyway. The hesitation is usually from worrying about the tradeoff.


## Wearing Earplugs Won't Cost You Your Situational Awareness


Riders worry earplugs will make it harder to hear what's happening around them. But earplugs can help improve your situational awareness on the road. A 1993 study testing riders' ability to detect warning signals found that[adding earplugs "led to significant reductions in minimum detection levels" at 40 mph and above](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8054899/) . Once wind roar is in the mix, earplugs make traffic sounds easier to pick out, because your ears aren't straining through a wall of white noise anymore.


### You Still Hear Your Own Bike


You’ll still be able to hear your own bike. Filtered earplugs cut sound *level* , not *detail* . You still hear your engine, your gear changes, the car merging next to you, just without the volume slowly wearing your hearing down.


### The Long-Term Hearing Cost of Skipping Protection


You should be wearing earplugs every ride, not just the long ones. Noise-induced hearing loss affects an estimated 10 million American adults under 70, and by some estimates as many as 40 million, according to the[National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD)](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/noise-induced-hearing-loss) . Unlike most hearing conditions, it's entirely preventable, and it builds up gradually over years.


### Wind Noise Adds Fatigue Too


There's a fatigue side to this too.[Wind noise is a known contributor to rider fatigue](https://trid.trb.org/View/860043) on long rides . Cut the roar and you show up at your destination less wrecked: with steadier hands, a clearer head, and more of the ride still feeling good instead of gritted-out.


Earplugs lower overall noise volume, not specific warning frequencies, and in controlled testing, riders wearing earplugs detected sirens and horns more reliably above 40 mph than riders without them.


With the worry of losing situational awareness off the table, the next thing most riders want to know is, is wearing earplugs while riding even legal?


## Is It Legal to Wear Earplugs While Riding a Motorcycle? Yes, With One Exception


In the great majority of U.S. states, wearing earplugs while riding a motorcycle is legal, with one catch. Laws restricting in-ear devices mostly target audio, headphones and earbuds playing music, not hearing protection. Wear plain earplugs and you're covered in most states,[though a handful like Alaska restrict noise-blocking earplugs](https://www.motorcyclelegalfoundation.com/is-it-illegal-to-wear-headphones-on-motorcycles-a-state-by-state-guide/) more broadly regardless of whether you're playing audio.


Run music through both ears and that's where state law gets particular everywhere else.


### The California Example


[California Vehicle Code 27400](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=27400.&lawCode=VEH) prohibits headsets or earplugs covering both ears while driving or riding, but carves out an explicit exemption for "personal hearing protectors in the form of earplugs or molds that are specifically designed to attenuate injurious noise levels," provided they don't block your ability to hear a siren or horn.


### Check Your Own State's Law


Passive hearing protection is legal in the great majority of states, but audio playback in both ears is where the law varies most. Alaska has its own stricter earplug rule on top of that. This is general guidance, not legal advice, so confirm your own state's current law before riding with any in-ear device. A few minutes of checking beats a citation.


Hearing-protection earplugs aren't a regulated medical device, and no state requires a permit to wear them. Legally, the real difference comes down to passive protection versus in-ear audio playback.


With the legal question settled, the only real decision left is which earplugs to buy.


## Foam, Filtered, or Custom? How to Pick the Right Motorcycle Ear Plugs


With many earplug options on the market, it can be challenging to know where to start looking. Only three things decide whether a pair works for you: how much sound it blocks, how it fits under your helmet, and what type of filter it uses. Get those three right and the rest is just preference.


### NRR Tells You How Much Sound You're Blocking


NRR or Noise Reduction Rating measures how many decibels an earplug blocks under lab conditions. For street riding, stay in the high-teens to low-20s NRR range (upper-20s SNR). More isn't automatically better, no matter how tempting that math feels. Go past 30 NRR and you can cut yourself off from traffic and your own bike entirely, which defeats the point of riding with your ears on.


### Fit Decides Whether You'll Wear Them


You know the feeling: twenty minutes in and you're already thinking about the thing pressing against your ear. That's a fit problem, not a noise problem, and it's the real reason a good pair of earplugs ends up in a drawer instead of your ears. Look for a low-profile stem that clears your helmet's cheek pads, no hard edges building a pressure point over a few hours, and a design where you can sit one-handed with gloves half off.


### Filter Type Decides How Much You Still Hear


The four stack up like this:


Filter Type Attenuation Detail Retention All-Day Comfort Cost


Basic foam High Low Medium $


Filtered / high-fidelity Medium-High High High $$


Custom molded High High Highest $$$


Electronic (Bluetooth/hear-through) Adjustable Highest High $$$$


A few comfort checks before you buy: silicone tips wash and reuse easily, foam tips wear out faster and need replacing sooner, and a tether or hard case keeps a spare pair from vanishing into your tank bag eventually.


NRR, fit, filter type: that's the whole framework, and it's exactly what AXIL builds its motorcycle lineup around.

## Why Your Concert Earplugs Won't Cut Motorcycle Wind Roar


Concert earplugs are built to take the edge off a wall of sound: a snare hit, a guitar stack, a crowd. Motorcycle wind noise works differently. It's a sustained, low-frequency roar that calls for a different kind of earplug. Foam and deep-seal silicone earplugs outperform shallow "lifestyle" plugs specifically at low frequencies, because[blocking a low-frequency sound takes a longer, tighter seal in the ear canal than blocking something sharp and high-frequency](https://www.osha.gov/otm/section-3-health-hazards/chapter-5) .


### Cruisers and Naked Bikes Catch More Wind


Riding a Harley, a cruiser, or a naked bike? You're catching more wind than a sport-tourer rider at the same speed. Less fairing and less windscreen coverage means more airflow hits your helmet directly, instead of getting broken up first. That's the gap between needing solid hearing protection and needing it *now* .


### Stack a Windscreen, Seal, and Wind Filter With Your Earplugs


A few things stack with earplugs to cut wind noise further: a taller or better-angled windshield, a tighter helmet seal, a balaclava or neck gaiter to kill turbulence at your collar. ISVR's wind-tunnel testing found that[windscreen and helmet-seal adjustments cut helmet noise by 5–8 dB](https://isvr.co.uk/noise-levels-under-motorcycle-helmets/) , a real drop before your earplugs even do their part. Already running earplugs and still catching a roar past them? Try the[AXIL Wind Filter](https://goaxil.com/products/wind-filter?_pos=1&_sid=4f2e27a56&_ss=r) next. It won't fix a bad fit or the wrong filter type, but once those are dialed in, it closes the gap.


None of this rules out riding with music or GPS turned on. It just changes how you should do it.


## Motorcycle Ear Plugs With Bluetooth and Speakers: The Right Way to Ride With Music


Standard earbuds and helmet speakers back you into the same corner every time: to beat 90+ dB(A) of wind noise, you turn the volume up, stacking hearing damage on top of the wind exposure you already had.


### Active Noise Cancellation Isn't Hearing Protection


ANC doesn't fix it either, even though it sounds like it should. ANC makes constant background noise *sound* less noticeable, but it doesn't physically block sound pressure the way passive hearing protection does. ANC headphones are not hearing protection, full stop. Read more on[why noise cancellation isn't the same as protection](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/cancellation-vs-protection?srsltid=AfmBOopaxxaR4S2XHaaFsu2PPcZQXzspHeQybuFetYsgtjGcwxPUmkSQ) .


### Block the Wind First, Then Add Sound


That's the right order, and it's how the[GS Extreme 3.0](https://goaxil.com/products/gs-extreme-3-0?_pos=1&_sid=f3421583c&_ss=r) works: isolation handles the wind passively before Bluetooth ever kicks in, so your music, calls, or GPS cues sit at a genuinely safe volume instead of the loudest you can stand over the wind. You shouldn't have to choose between hearing your directions and protecting your hearing.


Running Bluetooth audio in both ears? Re-check the legality section above. That's the specific scenario where state law varies. Passive plugs alone are a simpler question.


## Frequently Asked Questions About Motorcycle Ear Plugs


What NRR do motorcycle earplugs need?


High-teens to low-20s NRR (upper-20s SNR) covers most street speeds. Riding sustained highway miles or a naked bike with more wind exposure? Lean toward the higher end of that range.


Can you wear earplugs under a full-face motorcycle helmet?


Yes. A low-profile earplug seats fully in your ear canal without pressing against your helmet's cheek pads.


Do motorcycle earplugs block sirens and horns?


No. Earplugs lower overall volume, not specific frequencies, so warning sounds stay distinguishable. One controlled study found[earplugs improved warning-signal detection above 40 mph.](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.3109/03005369309076718)


Are custom molded earplugs worth it for motorcycle riding?


For comfort, yes, and if fit has been a fight for you before, that comfort is worth real money. For attenuation, a quality universal-fit filtered earplug performs comparably for a fraction of the price.


How often should you replace motorcycle earplugs?


Foam earplugs wear out fast, so replace them often. Silicone and filtered earplugs last longer: wash them, check the seal, skip the fixed replacement schedule.


Can a passenger use the same earplugs as the rider?


Keep a dedicated pair for each of you, and stash a spare set of foam plugs for a passenger who forgot theirs. Plan for it once and you never have to think about it again.


What decibel level requires ear protection on a motorcycle?


NIOSH sets[85 dB(A) as the threshold for requiring hearing protection over an 8-hour exposure](https://www.osha.gov/noise) . Motorcycle wind noise clears that number before you even reach highway speed.


## The Real Cost of Skipping Motorcycle Ear Plugs


Skipping earplugs during your ride can be one of the worst things you do. Ear damage can show up as a ringing that never fully fades, then a "what?" you find yourself asking more than you used to. Highway wind noise regularly runs 90 to 112 dB(A) under your helmet, and it adds up ride after ride.


The fix can start at $2 for[a pair of foam plugs](https://goaxil.com/products/foam-ear-plugs-1?_pos=3&_sid=c24f82f00&_ss=r) and scales up from there, depending on how much protection and audio you want layered on top.


Three decisions carry the real weight here: the NRR you need for your typical speed, the fit under your specific helmet, and whether you want audio layered on top of protection. Get those three right, and you can stop thinking about your ears and get back to thinking about the road.
